sources_reopened.note: Abstract and text agree with the record (399 episodes, 147 with bacteriuria plus pyuria, RR 1.42 for change in character of urine). The 68/144 v 79/255 counts behind '47 v 31 in 100' sit in Table 3, which the tool does not return; they sum to the abstract totals (147 and 399), so they are internally consistent but the table itself was not re-read.
27/152 v 43/160 vaginal tissue figures confirmed; the paper gives no test or interval for them, and calls the outcome 'ulceration, granulation or other clinical concerns about the vaginal tissues'.

issues.text: Frailer people are more likely to be given pads (a Danish study of about 2,000 older patients found this), and they may also be more likely to leak. No observational study can fully remove that.
issues.problem: The claim that frailer people 'may also be more likely to leak' is not in any opened source; the Danish study (Larsen 2023) only shows frailer patients are more likely to become pad users. The caveat the record supports is about who is given pads.
issues.source_says: Larsen 2023: severely frail patients had higher odds of becoming pad users during admission (OR 1.57, 1.45 to 1.71); Zisberg adjusted for function, cognition, illness severity, age and length of stay.
issues.replacement: Frailer people are more likely to be given pads (a Danish study of about 2,000 older patients found this), so part of the link may reflect who is given pads rather than the pads themselves. No observational study can fully remove that.

issues.text: The same review found cranberry products probably reduce infections in children and in people prone to infection after a bladder procedure, and that stomach side effects were probably no more common than with placebo.
issues.problem: Confidence interval touching the null reported as equivalence: the review's gastrointestinal side-effect estimate is RR 1.33 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.77) against placebo or no treatment, so 'probably no more common' reads as a finding of no excess when a modest increase is compatible with the data. Also the comparator was placebo or no specific treatment, and the 'intervention' group is not limited to bladder procedures.
issues.source_says: Cochrane abstract: 'The number of participants with gastrointestinal side effects probably does not differ between those taking cranberry products and those receiving a placebo or no specific treatment (10 studies, 2166 participants: RR 1.33, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.77; moderate certainty)'. Children: RR 0.46 (0.32 to 0.68); people with a susceptibility to UTI due to an intervention: RR 0.47 (0.37 to 0.61).
issues.replacement: The same review found cranberry products probably reduce infections in children and in people prone to infection after a medical intervention, and reported that stomach side effects probably did not differ from placebo or no treatment, although the estimate (risk ratio 1.33, 95% confidence interval 1.00 to 1.77) leaves room for a modest increase.

issues.problem: Population narrowed: the review group is 'elderly institutionalised men and women' (care homes or other institutions, possibly including long-stay hospital settings); the X, LinkedIn and Threads versions say 'care homes or other institutions'.
issues.source_says: Cochrane: 'elderly institutionalised men and women (3 studies, 1489 participants: RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.30)'.
issues.replacement: For older people in care homes or other institutions, the trials showed no clear benefit

issues.text: The largest review of cranberry products (Cochrane, 2023) pooled 50 trials with 8,857 people.
issues.problem: 'Largest' is a superlative that no opened source states; the Cochrane abstract only gives the size of this fifth update.

issues.text: A larger US study found that a change in colour, smell or blood raised the chance of laboratory signs a little: about 47 in 100 against 31 in 100.
issues.problem: Population and setting qualifier missing from a headline number: the 47 v 31 figures come only from episodes in which staff already suspected a urine infection (399 episodes in 228 residents), are unadjusted, and the exposure was a combined 'change in character of urine' (visible blood, colour or odour), not colour or smell alone. Without this, the sentence reads as a general population finding.
issues.source_says: Juthani-Mehta 2009: 399 episodes of clinically suspected UTI in non-catheterised residents; bacteriuria plus pyuria in 68 of 144 episodes (47%) with a change in character of urine v 79 of 255 (31%) without; adjusted RR 1.42 (1.07 to 1.79). The paper notes only clinically suspected cases were evaluated.
issues.replacement: A larger US study of residents already suspected of having an infection found that a change in the urine's colour, smell or blood raised the chance of laboratory signs of infection a little: about 47 in 100 against 31 in 100.

issues.text: In a French survey of 444 urine infections treated in 134 nursing homes, smelly urine was given as a reason in about 3 in 10.
issues.problem: Calls the 444 episodes 'urine infections'; they were reported (supposed) diagnoses of treated UTI, and the same paper found 21% of diagnoses rested on erroneous criteria and only 10% were consistent with guidelines.
issues.source_says: Lemoine 2018: 'Of 397 contacted facilities, 134 participated and informed 444 UTI episodes. Reported diagnostic criteria were burning urination (32%), malodorous urine (29%)... Twenty-one percent of diagnoses were based on erroneous criteria.'
issues.replacement: In a French survey of 444 treated episodes of suspected urine infection in 134 nursing homes, smelly urine was given as a reason in about 3 in 10.

issues.text: Ask whether antibiotics are being suggested for smell or colour alone.
issues.problem: The record's qualification that people with a catheter or who cannot report symptoms need separate judgement is in LinkedIn and the visual but missing from X, Bluesky and Threads.
issues.source_says: Stone 2012: criteria are for surveillance and 'may not be adequate for real-time case finding, diagnosis, or clinical decision making'; separate criteria apply to residents with a catheter.
issues.replacement: Ask whether antibiotics are being suggested for smell or colour alone. People with a catheter, or who cannot say how they feel, need a clinician's judgement.

issues.text: Once a day is the most common bowel pattern, but in a Bristol study only 40 in 100 men and 33 in 100 women kept to a daily cycle. Among adults with normal bowels, nearly all go between 3 times a day and 3 times a week. Tell your GP about a lasting change, blood or weight loss.
issues.problem: Compression made the claim stronger and dropped necessary qualifications: 'adults with normal bowels' drops that the US figure is of people who called their own bowels normal (so it is not a cut-off), the Bristol study date is lost, and the age limit (adult studies, none covering people in their 80s or 90s, the likely audience) appears in every other version but not here.
issues.source_says: Mitsuhashi 2018: 95.9% of 4,775 US adults who reported normal bowel patterns had 3 to 21 movements a week; Walter 2010: 98% of 124 healthy Swedish adults aged 18 to 70; neither covers people over about 70.
issues.replacement: Once a day is the most common bowel pattern, but in a Bristol study only 40 in 100 men and 33 in 100 women kept to a daily cycle. Adults who called their bowels normal nearly all went 3 a day to 3 a week. Not studied in people in their 80s. Tell your GP about a lasting change, blood or weight loss.

issues.text: and fewer had sore or damaged vaginal skin on examination (about 18 in 100 against 27 in 100).
issues.problem: 'Sore or damaged vaginal skin' is not what was measured: the outcome was ulceration, granulation or other clinical concerns about the vaginal tissues (including atrophy and redness). The paper reports no test or interval for the 27/152 v 43/160 comparison (a rough calculation puts it near the edge of chance), it was a secondary outcome added to the protocol, and the denominators are the women examined (152 and 160 of 169 and 171). Presenting it as a headline result without that is imprecise.
issues.source_says: Hagen 2023 full text: 'Ulceration, granulation or other clinical concerns about the vaginal tissues (e.g., vaginal atrophy, erythema) on examination at 18 months were less common in the self-management group (27/152, 17.8% vs 43/160, 26.9%)'. No confidence interval or P value is reported for this secondary outcome, and vaginal tissue health was added to the secondary outcomes after registration.
issues.replacement: and fewer had ulceration or other concerns about the vaginal tissues on examination (about 18 in 100 against 27 in 100). The trial did not report whether that gap was larger than chance.

issues.text: Complications were again lower with self-management, but that difference was no longer statistically clear.
issues.problem: States lower complications at 4 years although the difference was not statistically clear; the record says not to claim fewer complications at 4 years. The reduced response (55%) and loss of power are the authors' explanation.
issues.source_says: Bugge 2025: 'a statistically non-significant lower percentage of pessary complications for SM (SM 17.7% vs CBC 22.0%, AMD 3.01, CI -0.58 to 6.61)'; 186 of 340 (55%) responded; 'loss of statistical power... may explain the lack of a statistical difference'.
issues.replacement: At 4 years the difference in complications was similar in size but no longer statistically clear, and only about half the women answered.

issues.text: Women who looked after their own pessary reported fewer pessary problems,
issues.problem: Necessary qualification missing: the complications measure was an unvalidated, self-completed questionnaire in an unblinded trial, and the difference was small (average 16.7% v 22.0% of relevant complication types).
issues.source_says: Hagen 2023: 'Participants, intervention deliverers, researchers and the statistician were not blinded'; adjusted mean difference -3.83 percentage points (95% CI -6.86 to -0.81); 'A validated pessary complications questionnaire needs to be developed'.
issues.replacement: Women who looked after their own pessary reported slightly fewer pessary problems (on a questionnaire, in a trial where women knew which group they were in),

issues.text: No clear difference in quality of life, fewer complications

issues.text: In hospital studies, reminders and automatic stop orders about halved the rate of catheter infections and shortened catheter use by about 2.6 days per patient.

issues.text: Three-panel illustrated strip, labelled not a real conversation. An older woman tells a practice nurse she has had some accidents with her bowels. He asks about her usual bowel pattern. He offers simple first steps and she asks if a continence service could help. Banner: about 15 in 100 US adults aged 70 and over at home reported leakage in a month; about 1 in 3 had talked to a doctor.
issues.problem: The 'about 1 in 3' figure is stated without the population and era the record requires: it comes from two US surveys of clinic patients in the 1990s and of women aged 45 and over, not from the older at-home adults in the 15 in 100 figure beside it (the visual and Threads put the two in one sentence).
issues.source_says: Johanson 1996: one-third of 881 clinic attenders (primary care and gastroenterology, Illinois, 1990s) with faecal incontinence had ever discussed it with a physician; Brown 2013: 29% (268/938) of US women aged 45 and over with accidental bowel leakage had sought care (mostly under 65, white, insured).
issues.replacement: Three-panel illustrated strip, not a real conversation. An older woman tells a practice nurse she has had some accidents with her bowels. He asks about her usual bowel pattern and offers simple first steps; she asks if a continence service could help. Banner: about 15 in 100 US adults aged 70 and over at home reported leakage in a month; in two other US surveys about 1 in 3 had talked to a doctor.

issues.text: European guidance tells doctors and nurses to ask about bowel leakage directly and to use words like "accidents".
issues.problem: Overstates the guideline: it says to take account of the person's preferred wording and gives 'accidents' as one example, not that clinicians should use that word.
issues.source_says: Assmann 2022 (UEG): 'Direct questioning rather than talking around the issue should be aimed for'; 'cultural preferences for wording should be taken into account (e.g. accidents, unwanted loss of faeces, etc.)'.
issues.replacement: European guidance tells doctors and nurses to ask about bowel leakage directly and to take account of the words a person prefers, such as "accidents".

issues.text: Leakage becomes more common with age. In a US national survey of adults living at home, about 3 in 100 people in their 20s reported any bowel leakage in the past month, rising to about 15 in 100 (roughly 1 in 7) of those aged 70 and over.
issues.problem: 'Becomes more common with age' reads as a change within people over time; the source is a one-time cross-sectional survey comparing age groups. The X version also omits that 'any leakage' includes small amounts of liquid or mucus (LinkedIn has it).
issues.source_says: Whitehead 2009 (NHANES 2005-06, n=4,308): leakage of solid, liquid or mucus at least once in the preceding month rose from 2.6% in 20 to 29 year olds to 15.3% in those aged 70 and over; noninstitutionalised adults.
issues.replacement: Leakage is more common in older age groups. In a US national survey of adults living at home, about 3 in 100 people in their 20s reported any bowel leakage in the past month (including small amounts of liquid or mucus), against about 15 in 100 (roughly 1 in 7) of those aged 70 and over.

issues.text: Many people improve, and there are further tests and treatments if not.
issues.problem: 'Many people improve with these simple steps' is not quantified and the record notes the evidence for each first step is modest (psyllium better than placebo; education alone did about as well as exercises or biofeedback in trials without an untreated control, so some improvement may be natural change).
issues.source_says: Assmann 2022 (UEG): first-line treatment includes dietary advice, toilet routine, bulking agents or anti-diarrhoeals, pelvic floor exercises and absorbent products; 'both groups improved in all outcomes compared to baseline' (no untreated control); 'An education pamphlet... may be effective... Results should be interpreted with caution.'
issues.replacement: These steps help some people, though the evidence for each is modest, and there are further tests and treatments if not.

issues.text: Care that works
issues.problem: Series label overstates the evidence for a headline built on a 75-man trial whose combined outcome was mostly screen-detected bacteriuria and was clear only after adjustment, a weaker (category II) guideline recommendation, and no clear difference in men with dementia. This is an option to weigh, not proven good care.
issues.source_says: Saint 2006: unadjusted P=.07; adjusted HR 2.26 (1.10 to 4.62); 'bacteriuria... was by far the most frequent'; CDC 2009 Category II.
issues.replacement: Weighing it up

issues.text: In a trial of 75 men in hospital, aged about 73 on average,
issues.problem: Setting omitted: the trial was in one US veterans' hospital (1997 to 2001), which affects how far it applies to UK older men.
issues.source_says: Saint 2006: 'An academically affiliated Veterans Affairs Medical Center'; male veterans aged 40 and older, August 1997 to March 2001.
issues.replacement: In a US trial of 75 men in a veterans' hospital, aged about 73 on average,

issues.text: In a 75-man trial it was more comfortable;
issues.problem: Overstated: comfort was reported by the men on a questionnaire (more likely to say comfortable and not painful), not measured, and there was no difference on restriction of movement, embarrassment or inconvenience.
issues.source_says: Saint 2006: 'patients with a condom catheter were more likely to report their device to be comfortable (P=.02) and not painful (P=.02)... On other measures of preference, there were no significant differences.'
issues.replacement: In a 75-man trial, more men said it was comfortable;

issues.text: In a trial of 75 hospital men it was more comfortable.
issues.problem: Same as Bluesky: self-reported comfort stated as a fact.
issues.source_says: Saint 2006: men with a sheath were more likely to report it comfortable (P=.02) and not painful (P=.02).
issues.replacement: In a trial of 75 hospital men, more of them said it was comfortable.

issues.text: Similar shares of men had an event (about 44 against 49 in 100).
issues.problem: The dementia subgroup result (no clear difference in men with dementia, with a chance imbalance in who got sheaths) is in the LinkedIn version but missing from X, Bluesky, Threads and the visual, although the post recommends considering a sheath for men generally.
issues.source_says: Saint 2006: dementia in 60.6% of the sheath group v 20.5% of the catheter group (by chance); difference 'not significantly different for those with dementia (P=.78)'.
issues.replacement: Similar shares of men had an event (about 44 against 49 in 100). In men with dementia the trial did not show a clear difference.
